meaning: Possibly 'grief of the people' (from ἄχος + λαός), or a pre-Greek name

pronunciation.approximation: ah-khil-LEWS, stress on the final syllable.
pronunciation.note: Homeric Greek Ἀχιλλεύς scans with a short i and a stressed final syllable; the geminate λλ is attested in the best manuscripts beside the single-λ variant Ἀχιλεύς. The restoration Achilleús keeps the acute on the final syllable exactly where the Greek puts it. In the epic hexameter the name scans ⏑ – —: a short first alpha followed by two long syllables, and that short first syllable is precisely why the single-λ variant Ἀχιλεύς exists.

domains.title: The Best of the Achaeans
domains.subtitle: War, Glory, Rage, and the Short Bright Life
domains.lead: Achilleús is the hero the Iliad is named around: the man who chose a short life with imperishable fame (kleos aphthiton) over a long life in obscurity. His wrath is the poem's first word — mēnin — and his heel is the world's oldest named weakness.

cards.name: The Wrath
cards.desc: The Iliad opens on his mēnis — a rage that costs the Achaeans thousands of lives and remakes epic poetry.

cards.name: The Heel
cards.desc: The single unarmoured point of an otherwise deathless fighter; the West's shorthand for a fatal flaw.

cards.name: Kleos Aphthiton
cards.desc: Imperishable fame — the bargain every brand strikes: burn briefly and be remembered forever.

cards.name: Leuke the White Isle
cards.desc: His afterlife island in the Black Sea, where sailors left offerings to the hero for a thousand years.

symbols.name: The heel
symbols.meaning: The mortal point in the immortal frame; vulnerability as destiny

mythology.lead: Son of the mortal Pēleús and the sea-goddess Thetis, Achilleús stands exactly between god and man: the strongest argument the Greeks ever made that excellence cannot cancel mortality.

myths.title: Two Fates, Weighed Aloud
myths.text: Book 9 of the Iliad stages the first great decision scene of Western literature. Agamemnon's embassy — Odysseus, Aias, and old Phoinix, bearing the offer of treasure, one of Agamemnon's daughters, and restored honor — finds Achilleús in his tent, singing “the famous deeds of men” to his lyre (9.186–189). His answer is the speech every later hero rehearses: his mother has told him he carries two fates — “if I stay here and fight around the city of the Trojans, my return home is lost, but my fame will be imperishable; if I sail back to my dear fatherland, my noble fame is lost, but my life will be long” (9.412–416). He refuses the gifts, unconverted even by Phoinix's tale of Meleager, and chooses, in effect, to wait for Patroklos. The scene matters because the choice is made aloud, with the cost stated first: Achilleús never trades his life by accident — he prices it, in public, every time.

myths.title: The Death of Patroklos
myths.text: When Patroklos begged to enter the fighting in Achilleús' armor, the hero warned him: drive the Trojans from the ships and come back — do not press on to Troy (16.87–96). Patroklos drove them, pressed on, and Hektōr killed him in the borrowed armor, prophesying with his dying breath that Achilleús would soon die beneath the same wall (16.816–854). Achilleús' grief was absolute: Thetis found him face-down in the dust, groaning, holding his head while he chose revenge and death together (18.23–126). Hephaistos forged him new armor — the shield whose rim is Ocean, the most famous description in Greek verse (18.468–613) — and he returned a changed thing, “raging, grim,” his own horses weeping for Patroklos (19.392–424). He killed Hektōr, tied the corpse to his chariot, and dragged it round his friend's tomb (22.395–404; 24.14–18) — until Priam came alone to the tent at night, kissed the hands that had killed his sons, and the two enemies wept together, one for Pēleús and Patroklos, one for Hektōr (24.468–676). The Iliad's argument completes itself here: wrath becomes grief, grief becomes pity, and the hardest man in the poem learns the one thing strength cannot seize.

myths.title: Paris' Arrow, the Heel
myths.text: The Iliad never tells Achilleús' death; it keeps only arranging the appointment. Hektōr, dying, foretells it — “the day will come when Paris and Phoibos Apóllōn destroy you at the Scaean gates” (22.358–360) — and the hero himself tells the doomed Lykāon that not even he will come home (21.110–113). The full story belonged to the lost Cypria, whose outline Proclus preserves: Achilleús, struck at the Scaean gates by Paris with Apóllōn guiding the shaft; a late variant sends him down in Apóllōn's own temple, marrying Polyksenē. The invulnerability is a Roman refinement: Statius, in the unfinished Achilleid (1.269–270), tells how Thetis dipped the infant in the Styx, so that every part of him “drank in deathlessness” except where her fingers covered his heel — and the spear that later grazed him there left a wound that would not close. The myth's precision is its point: the one mortal point of the deathless boy is the exact place his mother held — vulnerability as the footprint of love.

myths.title: The White Island
myths.text: The Odyssey's underworld gives Achilleús the most quoted anti-epitaph in Greek: better to be a living serf than king of the dead (Od. 11.488–491). But the Black Sea refused to leave him there. On Leukē, “White Island,” at the Danube's mouth, sailors believed the hero lived on — some said with Helen for his consort; Pausanias reports the belief as current in his own day (3.19.11–13), and Arrian's Periplus (21–23) describes the island's temple, its heaps of offerings, and the god appearing to sailors: a cult with a real address, provisioned for centuries. Around the Euxine he accumulated the title Pontarchēs, “Lord of the Pontus”: dedications to Achilleús Pontarchēs are known from Olbia and the surrounding coast, and Philostratus' Heroicus still has Protesilaos trading gossip about him with a Phoenician sailor. This is kleos aphthiton made literal — fame so successful it required real estate: an afterlife plotted, charted, and stocked by the sailors who needed him at the head of their sea.

lore.syncretism:
Rome read him through the Aeneid's mirror: Achilles is what Aeneas must not be — brilliant, doomed, and defiant of fate. Alexander the Great slept with the Iliad under his pillow and ran a victory lap around Achilleús' supposed tomb at Troy, consciously modelling his own short bright career on the hero's choice; his successors commissioned the Alexandrian portraiture of Achilles as the template of royal arete.

In late antiquity and Byzantium he survived as a romance figure — the Achilleid tradition and the Byzantine Achilleis kept him wandering long after Homer had closed his account — and in the Renaissance he returned as the measure of martial virtue. Modern Greece claims him as a national ancestor whose very untranslatability — rage, grief, honour — defines the epic imagination.
lore.culturalLegacy:
His name seeded two everyday terms: the Achilles heel (a single fatal weakness) and the Achilles tendon, named by the anatomist Verheyen in 1693 for the tendon nearest the mythic wound. "The wrath of Achilles" remains the standard translation exercise for every student of Greek, the μῆνιν ἄειδε θεά that begins Western literature.

Every sport that sells invincibility borrows his silhouette — until the heel reminds the audience how the story ends.
lore.extendedMeditation: Achilleús is the god of the deadline. He knows the exact price of brilliance and pays it anyway, and his story asks the reader which currency they are spending: years, or light. To hold his name is to hold the oldest question in the Western canon — whether a life is measured by its length or by what survives it.

lore.archaeology: A hero-cult of Achilleús is documented at his tomb in the Troad (the tumulus at Sivri Tepe) and, most vividly, on the island of Leuke off the Danube delta, where Arrian reports a temple, votive offerings, and the hero appearing to sailors. Vase painting made him one of the most depicted figures in Greek art: the François Vase shows his pursuit of Troilos, and the Achilles-and-Ajax dice game survives in dozens of black-figure cups, including Exekias' masterpiece. Roman-era stamps and lamps from Olbia confirm the Black Sea cult lasted centuries.
